newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solvay sees caustic soda price rise.
newsitem.headline: Solvay sees caustic soda price rise.

text.p: Belgian chemicals group Solvay said on Thursday it would not make any forecast for full-year earnings but that it had begun to push through price increases in caustic soda.
Solvay said earlier a sharp fall in caustic soda and hydrogen peroxide prices held net current earnings growth in the first half of 1997 to three percent to 6.1 billion Belgian francs.
"We are not making any forecast for the second half or for the whole of the year, departing Solvay chief executive officer Daniel Janssen told a news conference.
"We live in such erratic times, whether with products or currencies or economies that we don't want to make the slightest comment on the second half at this stage," Janssen said.
He said however the company had raised caustic soda prices in July and was "rather confident" of making a further price increase in September.
Janssen said Solvay was slightly behind U.S. chemicals group Dow Chemical, the world's largest caustic soda producer, which announced a $25/tonne increase in May.
"The trend is up for the margin on caustic soda. How high it will get for us or Dow is too hard to say at this time," Janssen said.

Solvay said the devaluation of the Thai baht against the U.S. dollar had effectively wiped out the possibility of the group benefiting in its consolidated accounts from the dollar's rise against the Belgian franc this year.
Janssen said however that any potential loss on dollar debt held by Vinythai, of which Solvay's share is 45 percent, had been entirely provisioned for in Solvay's first-half figures.
He said the provision was based on an exchange rate of 32 baht to the dollar.
Solvay said that if the baht recovered, its potential losses would decrease.
The spokeswoman noted however that if the baht continued to slide, a further provision might be necessary.
Janssen said the baht devaluation was a blow to Vinythai's balance sheet but was proving beneficial to its business.
"We are now selling PVC with lower costs in Thailand and on the international markets. Vinythai has sizeable dollar revenues," Janssen said.
"Vinythai is now break-even and making profit on a monthly basis," said Janssen, adding that profits should increase further due to the devaluation.
He noted that the baht's devaluation against the deutschemark/Belgian franc was much less than against the dollar.
